conventions.convention: The sphere is C together with infinity; the infinity chart sends finite z to 1/z and infinity to 0, while the chosen stereographic map sends infinity to the north pole.
The chordal metric is the full Euclidean chord length on the unit sphere, so its finite-coordinate formula has the factor 2.
The ordered cross-ratio is [(z1,z2);(z3,z4)]=((z1-z3)(z2-z4))/((z1-z4)(z2-z3)), with the four stated limiting conventions when one entry is infinity; quadruples are pairwise distinct.
Holomorphic normality requires a finite-valued holomorphic locally uniform subsequential limit; meromorphic normality instead permits a meromorphic chordal limit or the constant map infinity.

The canonical exhaustion starts at n=1, uses both |z|≤n and distance from the boundary at least 1/n, allows early stages to be empty, and assigns infinite boundary distance when the domain is all of C.
The exhaustion metric uses weights 2^(-n), truncates each stage supremum by min(1,s_n), and sets s_n=0 on an empty stage.
Montel's theorem and the chordal Arzelà–Ascoli criterion explicitly assume the Axiom of Choice, including Countable Choice and Dependent Choice for successive subsequence selection.
For rational maps, degree is max(deg P,deg Q) for a coprime representative, and fibre multiplicity includes any contribution at infinity in the 1/z chart.
The boundary coefficient ring is O_{0,0}=C with maximal ideal {0}.
Regularity and preparation are in the last variable z_m; order 0 is admitted, and a Weierstrass polynomial is monic in z_m with every lower coefficient vanishing at the parameter origin.
The zeroth power in the slice power-sum construction is the constant polynomial 1, so p_0 counts all d roots with multiplicity, including roots equal to 0.

A nonidentity Möbius map is parabolic with one fixed point or conjugate to z↦λz with two fixed points; the multiplier branches and projective invariant tr(A)^2/det(A) use the terminology stated there.

load_bearing.statement: Let f∈O_{m,0} be regular in z_m of order d. Then there are a unit u∈O_{m,0} and a Weierstrass polynomial W of degree d such that f=uW.
Let W be a Weierstrass polynomial of degree d in z_m. Every f∈O_{m,0} has a unique quotient q and unique remainder of z_m-degree <d upon division by W.
If F:U→C^m is holomorphic and det J_C F(a)≠0, then F is biholomorphic between neighbourhoods of a and F(a), and its inverse G satisfies DG(w)=DF(G(w))^(-1).
Let m≥1 and let f∈O_{m,0} be nonzero. Then there is an invertible complex-linear map T and an integer d≥0 such that f∘T is regular in the last variable of order d.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let Ω be a plane domain and let F⊆H(Ω) be locally bounded. Then F is a normal family.
A map on the Riemann sphere is meromorphic if and only if it is rational: on the finite chart it is P/Q for coprime polynomials P,Q, not both zero, and it is not identically infinity.

A chordally locally uniform limit of meromorphic functions on a plane domain is meromorphic or identically infinity; if every approximant is holomorphic, the limit is holomorphic or identically infinity.
For any ordered triples of distinct sphere points, there is a unique Möbius transformation carrying the first triple to the second.

Assuming Choice, a family of meromorphic maps is meromorphically normal if and only if its restrictions are chordally equicontinuous on every compact subset; it is enough to check the canonical exhaustion stages.

concerns.concern: The item takes f:V→C with infinity in V and writes f(phi_infinity^(-1)(w))=f(1/w) at w=0. The latter expression is not defined unless 1/0=∞ is explicitly declared, and a C-valued function already defined at infinity cannot literally have that full chart expression be a pole there. The pole clause needs a punctured-domain or sphere-valued formulation.

The claimed equivalent infinity clause is too weak when f(infinity) is finite: it asks only that w↦f(1/w) be meromorphic at 0, not holomorphic with value f(infinity). For example, the finite-chart function f(z)=z with f(infinity)=0 satisfies that bullet through 1/w but is not holomorphic at infinity.

The definition quantifies over arbitrary functions Ω→C. Such functions need not be bounded on compact K_n, so s_n can be +∞ rather than a real number; no extended-supremum convention is stated. Restricting to functions bounded on every stage, in particular continuous functions, would make the metric literal.

The refutation changes more than the unit condition: z_2^2=z_2·z_2 uses a prepared polynomial of degree 1, whereas uniqueness for a germ regular of order 2 compares degree-2 Weierstrass polynomials. If the degree-d condition is retained and only the unit hypothesis is dropped, the other factor is automatically nonzero at the origin, hence a unit. The witness therefore does not refute the stated claim in the precise preparation context.

The cited one-point-compactification theorem makes density conditional on noncompactness and Hausdorffness conditional on local compactness and Hausdorffness. The remark invokes both conclusions for C without supplying those elementary hypotheses.

Step 1.1 says limits preserve the inequalities but does not explicitly show that the limit remains in the open set Ω. One must use positive distance from the boundary to exclude a limit in ∂Ω; the Ω=C case is separate.

The theorem is stated for arbitrary functions, while its cited local-uniform/compact-convergence dictionary is stated only for continuous maps. The equivalence itself extends by the same finite-cover argument, but that extension is not stated or proved here.

Its key fact is cited from a theorem only about the canonical exhaustion, yet the corollary applies it to two arbitrary compact exhaustions. It also passes from equality of sequential convergence to equality of topologies without explicitly invoking metrizability. Both are standard repairs but absent.

The Cauchy-estimate citation requires holomorphy on a strictly larger disc than the contour radius. From the chosen closed disc inside Ω one must first use compact containment to choose that larger disc; the proof applies the estimate without recording this step.

The final sentence asserts that the reflection formula is independent of the normalizing Möbius map, but the computation only proves conjugacy after a chosen normalization. Independence additionally requires showing that every Möbius map preserving the extended real line commutes with complex conjugation, equivalently has real coefficients up to scale.

At a point with limit value infinity, step 1.2 only produces a holomorphic reciprocal g=1/f, which might vanish identically on a neighbourhood. To conclude that a non-identically-infinity limit is meromorphic everywhere, the proof must propagate any locally identically-infinity patch by the identity theorem and connectedness; step 3.1 omits this argument.

Step 2.1 uses the determinant of diag(A,conjugate A) as the product of the two block determinants. The cited triangular-matrix theorem covers entrywise triangular matrices, not a block-diagonal matrix with arbitrary square blocks, so the block determinant fact still needs a short derivation.

Fact L2 is phrased only for a complex-linear automorphism, but it is applied to DF(a) in the step intended to prove real invertibility. The underlying cited lemma actually states the determinant identity for every complex-linear map; the proof should invoke that full statement or separately use the determinant criterion for the complex matrix.

The constructed source coordinate has alpha(a)=(F'(a),a_y), and the target shear sends F(a) to (F'(a),0), not necessarily to 0. Thus the proof establishes the normal form near those points, while the statement writes it near 0; source and target translations are missing.

The definition checks independence of representatives but not closure: it never cites or derives that sums and products of holomorphic representatives are holomorphic. The published algebra proposition supplies exactly this missing justification.

The page treats natural-number degree 0 elsewhere, but the displayed degree-d expression literally mentions a_{d-1}; at d=0 this is a_{-1}. An explicit empty-lower-sum convention or degree-zero clause is needed.

Equality f=uW=vP holds only as a germ on a small z_m-neighbourhood. To infer that the entire degree-d polynomials W(z',·) and P(z',·) have the same root multisets, the proof must first shrink the parameter neighbourhood so all their roots remain in that common z_m-disc.

The uniqueness step says a polynomial of degree <d that equals a holomorphic multiple of W is polynomially divisible by W. This is valid after observing that all d roots of W remain in the common disc and force the lower-degree polynomial to vanish with multiplicity, but that root-localization argument is omitted.

The final irreducibility equivalence silently assumes that every nontrivial polynomial factorization of a Weierstrass polynomial can be normalized into positive-degree Weierstrass factors. This follows from monicity, the local coefficient ring, and reduction at z'=0, but neither direction is shown before the equivalence is used by the UFD theorem.

Step 3.1 lets z' approach 0 while retaining only the fixed bound |z_m|<r, which alone does not show the resulting zeros approach the origin. The proof must either choose r arbitrarily small for each target neighbourhood or invoke continuity of the roots of the prepared polynomial.

The body correctly treats the complex hypersurface z_1^2+z_2^2=1, but the title calls it the unit circle. The real unit circle is not itself the complex holomorphic graph produced by the implicit-function theorem; the title should say the complexified circle equation or complex quadric.
